title: Dill-Cured Gravlax
description: A side of salmon buried in salt, sugar, and dill for two days. No heat touches it — the cure does all the work — and it keeps a week once sliced. Served as a starter for ten with a sweet mustard sauce.
notes: The salt-to-sugar ratio is the recipe. Roughly equal by volume gives a cure that seasons rather than pickles; push the salt up and you get something closer to lox, which is a different thing entirely.

ingredients.name: salmon fillet
ingredients.note: skin on, about 1 kg, pin bones out

steps.text: Run a fingertip down the centre of the salmon fillet against the grain and pull out every pin bone you find with tweezers.
steps.tip: Do this before the cure, not after. Cured flesh tears where a bone comes out and the slices show it.

steps.text: Mix the sea salt, sugar, and crushed white peppercorns, then work the chopped dill and the aquavit through until the whole lot is damp and green.
Lay the fillet skin down on a large sheet of cling film, pack the cure over every part of the flesh, and wrap it tightly enough that nothing can escape.
Set the parcel in a dish, weight it with a plate and two tins, and refrigerate. Turn it over once a day and pour off the liquid that collects.
steps.tip: The pooled liquid is the cure working, not a leak. Leave the fish sitting in it and the surface goes soft and grey.

steps.text: Unwrap, scrape the cure away with the back of a knife, and pat the surface dry.
Whisk the sweet mustard, Dijon mustard, white wine vinegar, and sugar together, then trickle in the neutral oil while whisking until it thickens to a pourable cream.
steps.tip: Trickle means trickle. Half the oil at once and the sauce splits into a slick you cannot bring back.

steps.text: Stir the finely chopped dill through the sauce and leave it to sit while you slice.
Slice the cured side thinly on a long shallow angle, starting at the tail, leaving the skin behind on the board.
steps.tip: A long flexible blade and slices you can almost read a newspaper through. Thick gravlax just eats salty.
